forces: Soprano solo, mixed chorus and orchestra with organ
performers: Lisa della Casa, soprano; Wiener Staatsopernchor; Wiener Philharmoniker; Franz Sauer, organ; Bruno Walter, conductor
recorded: Live, 26 July 1956, Small Festival Hall, Salzburg
question: Can returning music sound like an ending rather than a repetition?
intro: The ending looks back. In Süssmayr’s traditional completion, music from the Introitus and Kyrie returns with the Communion text: first the soprano’s prayer for light, then the choir’s intertwined fugue. Listen for what changes when familiar music carries new words. The file retains the live recording’s tail after the musical close.

sections.label: A · Light remembered
sections.mNote: The Introitus psalm music returns with Communion words

sections.label: B · Choral remembrance
sections.mNote: The later Introitus music returns to the choir

sections.label: C · Cum sanctis fugue
sections.mNote: The Kyrie’s paired subjects return with new text

sections.label: Close · Adagio

cues.title: An ending made from the beginning
cues.text: The Communion reuses music heard near the beginning of the Requiem. Its opening draws on the Introitus psalm verse, not the very first orchestral bars. Listen for a familiar kind of soprano line above an active string accompaniment.
cues.evidence: NMA p. 179 identifies Süssmayr’s adaptation of Mozart’s Introitus and Kyrie; compare Introitus p. 41. The report places a quiet instrumental opening before a rise near 0:15. This is a movement-level source relationship, not an aligned quotation marker.

cues.title: One line, many small movements
cues.text: The soprano’s line gives the opening a clear focal point, but the strings keep moving around it. Try following one of those quicker figures without losing the singer’s longer phrase: the two layers need not breathe at the same speed.
cues.evidence: NMA pp. 179–180; Breitkopf p. 95. The report’s changes around 0:26–0:38 fall within the opening solo span. This does not identify the singer’s precise entrance or individual notes.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The choir enlarges the prayer
cues.text: As the chorus takes over, the prayer acquires several registers and overlapping lines. The string motion survives the change of singer. Compare the crowded vocal texture with the exposed soprano line rather than listening only for an increase in volume.
cues.evidence: NMA pp. 181–183, choral continuation; Breitkopf pp. 95–96. The report rises around 0:45–0:55 and stays comparatively strong until 1:15. The 0:44 section boundary is provisional, not an aligned choral entrance.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The old prayer returns inside the new
cues.text: The later Introitus music returns too, including its interwoven plea for eternal rest. This is a larger act of recall than repeating one melody: the completion brings back a sequence of textures and the path they take towards a quiet close.
cues.evidence: NMA pp. 183–187 reprises the later Introitus material; compare pp. 45–48. The report withdraws at 1:20 and begins rebuilding around 1:30–1:40. This gives a broad location for the renewed prayer, not a text-aligned onset.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: What Süssmayr actually says
cues.text: In a letter dated 8 February 1800, Süssmayr explains that he repeats the Kyrie fugue at Cum sanctis to give the work unity. Constanze separately reports that Mozart wanted the first fugue repeated. The reported wish is not independent proof of a complete plan.
cues.evidence: Nowak’s NMA preface discusses Süssmayr’s letter to Breitkopf & Härtel and Constanze’s letter of 27 March 1799: https://dme.mozarteum.at/DME/objs/pdf/nma_14_-23_-3_eng.pdf. Their testimony and the surviving music are distinguished.

cues.title: Counterpoint before the fugue
cues.text: The voices are already overlapping well before the final fugue begins. Listen for phrases crossing one another while the strings reinforce their movement. A contrapuntal texture does not by itself mean that the Allegro fugue has started.
cues.evidence: NMA pp. 184–186 shows imitative Introitus-derived writing before the Allegro on p. 187. The report’s strong 2:05–2:15 and 2:30–2:40 spans lie before the major change at 3:18.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The first ending draws inward
cues.text: The broad choral passage withdraws into a quiet close before the faster music. Let that retreat register: the fugue will grow from renewed motion after a held threshold, not simply from an uninterrupted crescendo.
cues.evidence: Relative level drops from the strong 2:40 window to a low span around 2:50–3:10; novelty peaks at 2:48 and 3:18 bracket the withdrawal. NMA p. 187 supplies the held close before Allegro. The report alone does not identify its chord.

cues.title: Two subjects, two kinds of motion
cues.text: The final fugue combines a weightier subject with a quicker running line. Both come from the earlier Kyrie, now carrying the Communion text. Try hearing them as distinct characters that can coexist, rather than one melody with decoration underneath.
cues.evidence: NMA p. 187 begins the reused Kyrie double fugue at Allegro; Breitkopf pp. 98–104. The report’s 3:18 boundary and renewed level around 3:20 provisionally locate the start. Individual vocal entries are not aligned.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Keep the slower subject in view
cues.text: The running notes can capture the ear, but the broader subject gives the counterpoint its shape. Choose that less hurried line and follow it as other parts move around it. Urgency comes from the combination, not from every voice singing equally fast.
cues.evidence: The paired subjects and their contrasting note values are visible in NMA pp. 187–190. This is a listening strategy within the fugue, whose broad start is report-anchored near 3:18; it does not identify a specific singer at 3:50.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: A Salzburg concert in Mozart’s bicentenary
cues.text: The performance belongs to the Salzburg Festival of 1956, two hundred years after Mozart’s birth. Walter conducts the Vienna Philharmonic and Vienna State Opera Chorus, with Lisa della Casa singing the soprano passages. The venue is the Small Festival Hall.
cues.evidence: Vienna Philharmonic event archive: https://www.wienerphilharmoniker.at/en/konzerte/salzburg-festival/512/. Commons and upstream Internet Archive identify the choir; the 1756 birth year is given in the BSO work note. The bicentenary is a date comparison, not a claim about the concert’s stated dedication.

cues.title: The subject changes address
cues.text: Across the fugue, recognisable shapes move between high and low voices. Listen for identity surviving a change of register. The music develops through combinations and renewed entries, without needing a contrasting solo aria or a fresh orchestral theme.
cues.evidence: NMA pp. 190–194 shows the subjects distributed through the choral parts and doubled by instruments. The report maintains an active middle span without a comparable large break until the close. No individual entry is timestamped.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: The bass is an active participant
cues.text: Do not treat the lowest line as a stationary foundation. In this fugue it can carry thematic material while the upper voices answer or continue their running figures. Following the bass changes which part of the texture feels like the main argument.
cues.evidence: NMA pp. 193–196 includes subject material in the choral bass and instrumental bass lines. This is a passage-wide listening suggestion, not a claim that the audio analysis separates either bass part.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Gathering towards the last crest
cues.text: The closing stretch contains several renewed surges rather than one smooth crescendo. Keep the paired subjects in mind as the pressure builds: the strongest later statement is still made from the same contrapuntal material.
cues.evidence: The report has high relative-level windows around 5:25, 5:50 and especially 6:05–6:10. The score retains the paired subjects into the closing pages. The cue describes the broad approach, not an exact final entry.

cues.title: The running lines come to a stop
cues.text: The final Adagio replaces the running counterpoint with broad chords. The last sonority leaves D and A without a third: neither a smiling major chord nor a fully voiced minor one. Hear the openness of that ending after so many densely interwoven lines.
cues.evidence: NMA p. 199 and Breitkopf p. 104 show Adagio and the final open fifth. The report’s high 6:05–6:10 windows precede a marked spectral change at 6:20; the close is placed broadly before that retained recording tail, not at the 423.76-second file end.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Performance, issue and upload are different dates
cues.text: The performance is from 1956; the festival’s catalogue documents an Orfeo CD issue in 1996. Internet Archive receives this upload in 2018, followed by Commons. Those dates do not identify the carrier used for the transfer, its engineer or the recording’s first lawful publication.
cues.evidence: Salzburg Festival Festspieldokumente catalogue (2022), printed p. 138: Orfeo C 430 961 B, 1996. IA metadata gives 4 June 2018; Commons file history gives 5 June 2018. The cue sits in the retained tail and makes no claim of further score activity.

transitions.title: The solo prayer opens into the choir
transitions.how: The soprano’s adapted psalm phrase gives way to choral entries while the string figuration continues. Lower voices begin the choral continuation before the texture fills out above them. The change enlarges the number of active lines without discarding the accompaniment or introducing a new tempo. Süssmayr’s adaptation follows the Introitus sequence, making the remembered solo the doorway to a broader communal prayer.
transitions.evidence: NMA pp. 179–182; Breitkopf p. 95. The report’s 0:44 boundary and rise at 0:45–0:55 provisionally locate the choral expansion, not the separate bass, tenor or soprano entries.

transitions.title: A held dominant releases the fugue
transitions.how: The Introitus-derived music draws down to a held A-major dominant under a fermata. The Allegro then restores D-minor motion with the Kyrie’s two contrasting subjects: a weightier line and a running companion. The join changes tempo and contrapuntal activity after a genuine pause in momentum. The music is familiar from an earlier movement, but the new Communion words turn its return into the work’s closing argument.
transitions.evidence: NMA p. 187, slow close and Allegro; Breitkopf pp. 97–98. The report’s quiet 2:50–3:10 span gives way to a strong 3:18 boundary and rising level at 3:20. The dominant and subject relationship are read from the score, not estimated from chroma.

transitions.title: Running counterpoint becomes a broad final chord
transitions.how: The fugue’s moving lines are brought into broad Adagio chords. Sustained notes and a fermata interrupt the running subdivisions before the final cadence. The last D-and-A sonority omits the third, leaving the ending bare after the dense counterpoint. Its written close belongs before the remaining live-recording tail; that tail is not an additional musical coda.
transitions.evidence: NMA p. 199 and Breitkopf p. 104 show the closing Adagio and open fifth. The report’s strongest late windows at 6:05–6:10 precede a spectral boundary at 6:20; 6:00 marks a provisional closing span, not a bar-aligned tempo change. No orchestral activity is assigned to the later tail.

source.title: Mozart–Süssmayr Requiem, Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Dover unabridged reprint
source.locator: Printed pp. 95–104, checked against NMA pp. 179–199. Passage-level states estimated from the report, not aligned entrances or continuous activity. Basset horns lack a stage token; they are not relabelled clarinets. Trombones are withheld because Walter’s reported doubling cuts cannot be mapped to this session.

timeline.note: A short low-wind and string link recalls the Introitus psalm preparation; the unrepresented basset horns carry an important part of it.
The soprano’s Communion text lies over active strings and a reduced low line, as in the earlier psalm music.
The choir replaces the soloist in an expanding texture; the quicker string figures continue beneath the vocal lines.
The later Introitus-derived prayer gathers full choral weight, with intermittent brass and timpani punctuation.
The slow closing passage withdraws towards a held dominant; the groups describe the whole scored span, not continuous tutti sound.
The double fugue begins with interlocking choral lines and instrumental doublings; the two subjects have different rhythmic profiles.
The closing fugal span combines the subjects across registers; brass and drums add punctuation rather than a new theme.
The final Adagio broadens the ensemble into chordal writing and ends on an open fifth.
The report marks a sharp spectral change after the estimated musical close. The retained live-recording tail is not assigned instrumental activity.

fields.label: Performers
fields.value: Lisa della Casa (soprano), Wiener Staatsopernchor (chorus), Wiener Philharmoniker (orchestra), Franz Sauer (organ), Bruno Walter (conductor)
fields.note: Lisa della Casa is the soprano soloist for this movement. Commons and Internet Archive name the Wiener Staatsopernchor; the festival catalogue uses Konzertvereinigung Wiener Staatsopernchor. The primary concert archive confirms Walter, the orchestra, all four concert soloists and Franz Sauer, but leaves its choir field blank. Ira Malaniuk, Anton Dermota and Cesare Siepi belong to the full concert cast, not to an invented solo entrance in this movement.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Traditional Süssmayr Communio, adapting Mozart’s Introitus and Kyrie; performing edition and Walter’s alterations unidentified.
fields.note: The NMA labels the movement Süssmayr after Mozart’s Introitus and Kyrie. This is not an independently completed final movement in Mozart’s surviving manuscript. Süssmayr’s 1800 letter explains reuse of the Kyrie fugue; Constanze’s reported instruction from Mozart is testimony, not independent verification of a complete plan. File duration includes a retained live-recording tail after the estimated musical close.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: The primary concert archive identifies Thursday 26 July 1956; Commons, Internet Archive and the discography agree. This is the live performance date, not the date of first publication, a later commercial issue, digitisation or upload.

composer.epithet: An opera composer whose instrumental music gives different voices the freedom to disagree.
facts: By his father Leopold; extensive performing tours from childhood
Salzburg · Italy · Mannheim and Paris · Vienna from 1781
Italian opera seria and opera buffa; German Singspiel with spoken dialogue

composer.background:
Mozart was born in Salzburg in 1756, the seventh child of Leopold Mozart and Anna Maria Pertl; only he and his sister Maria Anna survived infancy. Leopold was a violinist and composer in the archbishop’s service, and in the year of Wolfgang’s birth published an influential violin treatise. He taught both children. Maria Anna, called Nannerl within the family, became an accomplished keyboard player, and the first tours presented brother and sister together. The family’s travels were an educational system as well as a business: the children encountered instruments, performers, repertories and audiences that a Salzburg childhood alone could not have supplied.

The long tour of 1763–66 took them through German courts, Paris, London and the Netherlands. In London Mozart met Johann Christian Bach, whose clear phrases and Italianate melodic style offered a model different from the contrapuntal teaching associated with Bach’s father. Illness repeatedly interrupted the itinerary. Leopold managed engagements, publicity and money while supervising composition, and the surviving correspondence documents the costs and uncertainties behind the public demonstrations. Wolfgang learned to write for named performers and immediate occasions before he had an independent adult household.
